newsitem.title: MAURITANIA: Mauritania poll puts racial divide back on agenda.
newsitem.headline: Mauritania poll puts racial divide back on agenda.

text.p: Mauritania's ruling party has won a crushing victory in the nation's first truly multi-party national assembly election, drawing cries of fraud from some opposition rivals and sceptical shrugs from others.

Friday's poll gave the Moslem West African nation its first woman parliamentian, a ruling party member who is also a member of the Harratin community of slaves once held by the dominant Moorish community or their descendents.

But the rise of a new party championing the rights of black Africans and Harratins has put the racial divide which has plagued the former French colony since independence in 1960 firmly back on the political agenda.
"The two most dispossessed communities have come together," said Sarr Ibrahima, general secretary of Action for Change.
"We have become the first opposition force in the country. That is the most important thing at this stage," he told Reuters, adding the new party included a handful of Moors.

For opposition veteran Hamdi Ould Mouknass the rise of Action for Change puts the question of peaceful coexistence firmly back on the political agenda. "New forces are emerging which will affect national unity," he said. "An extremely poor class is insisting on making its voice heard."
Mauritania, a sparsely populated nation at the Atlantic fringe of the Sahara Desert, straddles Arab and black Africa.
Light-skinned Moors of Arab stock and blacks each make up a third of the population, Arabic-speaking ex-slaves the remainder. Mauritania formally banned slavery in 1980.

The rivalry between Moors and black Mauritanians spilled over into tension with neighbour Senegal and bloodshed in 1989, with migrant Moors and Harratins killed in race riots in Senegal and reprisal killings in Mauritania.
Thousands of black Mauritanians fled to Senegal or were expelled. Senegal expelled Moors and Harratins.
Action for Change, formed a year ago, made a last-minute decision to seek a place in the 79-seat national assembly.
Like the rest of the opposition it failed to win a seat on Friday but it goes into an October 18 second round with a chance of winning five -- the best opposition performance.

Politicians say that for the first time the Harratin, who historically consider themselves part of the Arab community and make common cause with the Moors, have broken with tradition by joining blacks from the south in an alliance.

The ruling Democratic and Social Republican Party, which supports President Maaouya Ould Sid'Ahmed Taya and in which Moors are dominant, won 60 seats outright on Friday and the chance of 16 others in the run-off.
Delighted party officials described their victory as evidence that they alone enjoy a truly national following but acknowledged the scale of their win looked excessive.

"The absence of the opposition in the assembly is not good for democracy," said former prime minister Sidi Mohamed Ould Boubacar, general-secretary of the ruling party. "We are keen to see the opposition represented."

After previous election victories ruling party militants took to the streets to celebrate. On Saturday, the streets of the capital Nouakchott remained quiet and calm -- although extra police were deployed at main crossroads.
Taya, a French-trained army colonel, seized power in a bloodless coup in 1984. He launched a multi-party transition in 1991 and won a six-year term as president a year later.
The opposition boycotted the first multi-party legislative election in 1992. The ruling party won 67 seats.
The opposition was hoping to make its mark on Friday ahead of a presidential election due by January 1998.

But its supporters, many of whom expressed irritation at the heavy security force presence at polling stations, said problems over voting cards stopped many people voting and accused their rivals of sponsoring multiple voting.
Half Mauritania's 2.2 million people were eligible to vote. Turnout in Nouakchott was around 30 percent, much higher in the north and east, Taya strongholds.
Veteran opposition heavyweight Ahmed Ould Daddah was angry and bitter. "There was massive fraud organised by the state which took away all significance of the election," he said.
His Union of Democratic Forces-New Era party lost seats in two southern strongholds and in two in Nouakchott.
It has yet to decide whether or not to boycott Friday's run- offs, in which it is in the running for two seats.
Poll organisers and officials acknowledged problems with voting cards -- mistyped names or identity card numbers -- but blamed administrative inadequacies.

A small team of international observers highlighted "a number of imperfections", saying problems with voting cards and the use of indelible ink to prevent multiple voting should be addressed before the second round.
But for Mouknass, a former foreign minister, the elections are over. He will advise his supporters to vote for Action for Change, in line with a pre-poll agreement.
But he says the ruling party and president have to address the problems raised by the rise of Action for Change.
"The matter must be managed with much sensibility and patience," he said, advocating dialogue as the only solution.
